items.title: 7.4.1 Applications of Combination in Real Life

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: In everyday life we often choose a few things from many and do not care about the order: fruits for a chart, players for a team, questions to attempt in an exam, toppings for a pizza. Each of these is a combination, so we count it with \({}^{n}C_{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\). The two examples below show how.

blocks.title: Example 9
blocks.problem: Zain has 8 different fruits. He wants to select 5 fruits out of 8 fruits to make a fruit chart. How many combinations of fruits he can select?
steps:
Given: 8 different fruits; 5 are to be selected.
To find: the number of different selections of 5 fruits.
Method: a fruit chart needs only which fruits are chosen, not their order, so this is a combination with \(n = 8\) and \(r = 5\).

Step 1: Write the formula and put the values
\[{}^{n}C_{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\]
\[{}^{8}C_{5} = \dfrac{8!}{5!\,(8-5)!} = \dfrac{8!}{5!\,3!}\]
Why: \(n = 8\) fruits in all, \(r = 5\) are chosen.

Step 2: Open \(8!\) down to \(5!\) and cancel
\[= \dfrac{8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5!}{5!\;3!}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{3 \times 2 \times 1}\]
Why: \(8! = 8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5!\), so the \(5!\) on top and bottom cancel; \(3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1\).

Step 3: Simplify
\[= 8 \times 7 = 56 \text{ ways}\]
Why: \(3 \times 2 = 6\) cancels the 6 on top.

Check:
Choosing 5 fruits to put in is the same as choosing 3 fruits to leave out: \({}^{8}C_{3} = \frac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = 56\). The same answer.
blocks.answer: Zain has 56 different ways to select 5 different fruits to make a fruit chart.

blocks.title: Example 10
blocks.problem: In a school, a class consists of 12 girls and 8 boys. The teacher wants to select 5 students for an activity. In how many ways can the students be selected including? (i) 2 girls (ii) 5 boys (iii) 2 boys
steps:
Given: 12 girls and 8 boys; 5 students are to be selected.
To find: the number of selections with (i) exactly 2 girls, (ii) exactly 5 boys, (iii) exactly 2 boys.
Method: a group for an activity is a selection, so we use combinations. When the group has girls and boys, choose the girls and the boys separately and multiply (fundamental principle of counting).

Step 1 (i): Exactly 2 girls
5 students with 2 girls means 2 girls and 3 boys.
\[({}^{12}C_{2})({}^{8}C_{3}) = \dfrac{12!}{2!\,10!} \cdot \dfrac{8!}{3!\,5!}\]
\[= \dfrac{12 \cdot 11 \cdot 10!}{2 \cdot 10!} \cdot \dfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5!}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 5!}\]
\[= 66 \times 56 = 3696\]
Why: the 2 girls come from 12 girls (\({}^{12}C_{2} = 66\) ways) and the other 3 places must go to boys, chosen from 8 (\({}^{8}C_{3} = 56\) ways). Each choice of girls can go with each choice of boys, so we multiply.

Step 2 (ii): Exactly 5 boys
All 5 students are boys, chosen from 8 boys.
\[{}^{8}C_{5} = \dfrac{8!}{5!\,(8-5)!} = \dfrac{8!}{5!\,3!}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5!}{5! \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = 56\]
Why: no girl is selected, and \({}^{12}C_{0} = 1\), so only the boys' choice counts.

Step 3 (iii): Exactly 2 boys
5 students with 2 boys means 2 boys and 3 girls. The book's working is
\[({}^{8}C_{2})({}^{12}C_{3}) = \dfrac{8!}{2!\,6!} \cdot \dfrac{12!}{3!\,9!}\]
\[= \dfrac{8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6!}{2 \cdot 6!} \cdot \dfrac{12 \cdot 11 \cdot 10 \cdot 9!}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 9!}\]
and the book ends with \(({}^{8}C_{2})({}^{12}C_{3}) = 36960\). Simplifying each factor correctly:
\[{}^{8}C_{2} = \dfrac{8 \cdot 7}{2} = 28\]
\[{}^{12}C_{3} = \dfrac{12 \cdot 11 \cdot 10}{6} = 220\]
\[28 \times 220 = 6160\]
Why: 2 boys from 8 and 3 girls from 12, multiplied. The printed 36960 is 6 times too big: the \(3! = 6\) in the denominator was not divided out.

Check:
(i) and (iii) can be checked by a second route. In (i) the boys' part \({}^{8}C_{3} = 56\) equals \({}^{8}C_{5}\), which is the answer of (ii). In (iii) \(28 \times 220\) also equals \(28 \times {}^{12}C_{9}\) because \({}^{12}C_{3} = {}^{12}C_{9} = 220\). A computer count of all 5-student groups of the class gives exactly 3696 groups with 2 girls and 6160 groups with 2 boys.
blocks.answer: (i) 3696 ways  (ii) 56 ways  (iii) 6160 ways (the book prints 36960; see the correction below).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 10(iii): the book prints \(({}^{8}C_{2})({}^{12}C_{3}) = 36960\). The correct value is \({}^{8}C_{2} \times {}^{12}C_{3} = 28 \times 220 = 6160\). (36960 is \(6 \times 6160\): the \(3!\) in \(\frac{12!}{3!\,9!}\) was not divided.)

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text: A restaurant offers 6 flavours of pizza. How many ways are there to select 2 flavours of pizza?

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
For the Challenge: choosing 2 flavours is a selection (chicken-fajita with tikka is the same as tikka with chicken-fajita), so
\[{}^{6}C_{2} = \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2 \times 1} = 15\]
There are 15 ways.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Words like "including 2 girls" in this book mean exactly 2 girls (and the rest boys). Write the split first, for example "2 girls + 3 boys", then write one \({}^{n}C_{r}\) for each part and multiply. The numbers on top add up to the class (\(12 + 8 = 20\)) and the numbers below add up to the group (\(2 + 3 = 5\)): a quick way to see that nothing is missing.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Selecting a group from a larger set, with order not mattering, is \({}^{n}C_{r}\).
2. For a group made of two kinds (girls and boys), choose each kind separately and multiply.
3. \({}^{n}C_{r} = {}^{n}C_{n-r}\): choosing 5 to keep is the same as choosing 3 to leave.
4. Cancel the larger factorial before multiplying.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Adding instead of multiplying: \({}^{12}C_{2} + {}^{8}C_{3}\) is wrong. Girls AND boys are chosen together, so multiply.
2. Forgetting the other kind: for "2 girls" in a group of 5, the remaining 3 places must still be filled with boys.
3. Not cancelling the whole \(r!\): this is exactly the slip that turns 6160 into 36960.
